I have resolved the issue by updating `get_prefetch_queryset()` in [`ForwardManyToOneDescriptor`](file:///tmp/xhs-c6-host-2scph0ul/django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py#L120-L151), [`ReverseOneToOneDescriptor`](file:///tmp/xhs-c6-host-2scph0ul/django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py#L366-L383), and [`create_reverse_many_to_one_manager`](file:///tmp/xhs-c6-host-2scph0ul/django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py#L635-L655) within [django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py](file:///tmp/xhs-c6-host-2scph0ul/django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py).

### Cause
When prefetching a relation (one-to-one or reverse many-to-one), `get_prefetch_queryset()` eagerly evaluated the related `queryset` (after `Prefetch` lookups had been attached) and cached the parent `instance` back onto each `rel_obj` to populate the reverse relation cache. When `list(rel_qs)` was then evaluated in [`prefetch_one_level()`](file:///tmp/xhs-c6-host-2scph0ul/django/db/models/query.py#L1869-L1966), `_prefetch_related_objects()` ran on `rel_qs` first before `prefetch_one_level()` stripped `_prefetch_related_lookups`. Because the reverse relation was already cached on `rel_obj` with the parent `instance` (which had deferred fields), `prefetch_related_objects()` saw `is_fetched(obj) == True` and skipped assigning the newly prefetched instances, leaving the outer instance (with its deferred fields) cached on the related object.

### Fix
Only populate the reverse relation cache on `rel_obj` in `get_prefetch_queryset()` if `instance` does not have any deferred fields (`if not instance.get_deferred_fields():`).
